rationale: A wins because it has the better newsroom architecture: regulatory risk, study-design scrutiny, category shift, and subscription economics are four real doors, not four costumes on the same product blurb. Its best line, "Eight Sleep is running a study on its own mattress. Here's what the research design should tell you," turns the no-results clinic partnership into a reporter-shaped question. B is cleaner on evidence, but keeping "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking" as a live angle is a soft spot; marketing to a cohort is not proof that cohort is the story.
gaps_in_A: "low overnight blood oxygen is the primary marker of sleep apnea" is overconfident medical framing not supplied in the update; it needs a clinician or citation before it goes anywhere near a health reporter.
"On a $3,000 mattress" invents a precise price when the update only says the product costs several thousand dollars. Cute number, bad habit.
"the funding and methodology haven't been disclosed" asserts nondisclosure rather than saying those details were not provided here. That is how a smart angle becomes a fact-check problem.
"the exact fact pattern that draws FDA warning letters" overstates the regulatory risk. The concern is real; the warning-letter claim is not grounded in the supplied facts.
gaps_in_B: "Why athletes and biohackers are the test market for blood-oxygen sleep tracking" keeps a customer-story angle on one thin fact: the company markets to them. No named user, no usage data, no test-market evidence.

"A consumer-tech reporter at a gadget/reviews outlet" weakens the subscription-paywall angle. Reviews desks will review the bed; the sharper beat is subscription economics or consumer hardware business models.
It misses the strongest use of the clinic fact: the ongoing study with no results should become a research-design scrutiny angle, not just a warning against overclaiming validation.
"the cohort most willing to pay premium prices and parse overnight SpO2 trends" is plausible, but it is still an inference dressed as audience fact. Ask for proof before making that the pitch.
